### A Storm is Brewing - Is it Climate Change?

#### A Storm is Brewing. Is it Climate Change?

![A Storm is Brewing. Is it Climate Change?](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fd88e9fa2e08b696116873d43)

**Duration:** 00:32:29

**Released:** 2022

**Series:** How to Save a Planet

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/0KqTnupchaRay7qI7QuiKU)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/1KzrasExlM5dgMYwgFHns6)

For years, we were told it wasn’t possible to link specific weather events to global warming — and that made communicating about climate change difficult: When extreme weather events were in the news, climate change was often left out of the story. This week, we tell the story of how that changed. We talk to the scientists who figured out how to model the role of climate change in events like Hurricane Harvey — the climate detectives who blew the case of extreme weather wide open.Guests: Dr. Peter Stott, UK Met Office; Dr. Friederike (Fredi) Otto, Grantham Institute for Climate Change and the Environment; Dr. Stephanie Herring, NOAACalls to Action:  Help out climate scientists from your couch! Climate scientists rely on accurate weather data to produce and test their models. But lots of historical weather data is still locked away in handwritten records from the 1800s, like old ships’ logs. Now, you can help rescue that data — by transcribing old temperature and weather logs! Check out the project Weather Rescue, which connects volunteers with documents that need transcribing. Especially good if you're a pro at deciphering cursive handwriting...  Talk about the weather! If an extreme weather event linked to climate change occurs in your region, talk to your friends and family about how climate change is affecting the weather they’re experiencing. One goal of scientists like Fredi Otto is to help get climate science into the conversation — and that only works if people HAVE that conversation. People like you! Further Reading: You can find more information and recent studies on extreme weather events online at World Weather Attribution  Check out Dr. Fredi Otto's book about the development of rapid event attribution, Angry Weather, or Dr. Peter Stott's memoir about his experiences as a climate scientist, Hot Air  The American Meteorological Society publishes an annual round-up of the most interesting extreme weather event attribution studies, edited by Drs. Stephanie Herring and Peter Stott. If you liked this episode, you might like some of these past shows: Unnatural Disasters and How TV Weathercasters Went from Climate Skeptics to Champions. If you take an action we recommend in one of our episodes, do us a favor and tell us about it! We’d love to hear how it went and what it felt like. Record a short voice memo on your phone and send it to us via our Listener Mail Form. We might use it in an upcoming episode. Find all the actions we’ve recommended on our show here!Credits:How to Save a Planet is a Spotify original podcast and Gimlet production. It's hosted by Alex Blumberg.This episode was produced by Rachel Waldholz with help from Daniel Ackerman, Hannah Chinn and Nicole Welch. The rest of our reporting and producing team are Kendra Pierre-Louis and Anna Ladd.  Our supervising producer is Katelyn Bogucki. #### A call for redesigning American streets

![September 6, 2018: A call for redesigning American streets](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f66c44134aeaf736a7005e3c5)

**Duration:** 00:21:09

**Released:** 2018

**Series:** Better Off

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5tv31geSxNlyz9aGq1ivib)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

In this week’s podcast we’ll explore how America’s streets can be redesigned to benefit bicyclists and pedestrians—and we’ll explain why doing so may even help mitigate the effects of climate change. A new study from Anne Lusk, research scientist in the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzed how bicyclists and pedestrians responded to various placements of trees along cycle tracks—barrier-protected bicycle-exclusive paths between the road and the sidewalk. The research shows that the placement of these trees can play an important role in how people walking and biking perceive traffic, pollution, heat, and even safety. But the benefits extend beyond just those using the street—and could even be a factor in mitigating the effects of climate change. These trees may make it more likely that people will bike—helping to reduce pollution. And increased greenery can also help cool cities, which often suffer from a heat island effect, which means they’re significantly warmer than more rural areas. Lusk says all of this highlights the need to re-think how we’re designing streets to encourage more people to walk and bike instead of drive.

#### An Expert Vegetable Breeder On Innovating Crops For The Future

![An Expert Vegetable Breeder On Innovating Crops For The Future](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f85344bc437feeb218f3b7551)

**Duration:** 00:17:33

**Released:** 2024

**Series:** Science Friday

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/396ZL4TkV6YWWwFcpc0X8r)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/5UpA5Uw23B6bukC0TABffC)

It’s become clear to farmers and home gardeners alike that climate change is affecting the gardening landscape, literally. The climate is warming, pests are moving into different regions, and there’s a growing need for vegetable varieties that are resilient to the stresses of this new age.In the world of organic farming, the job of creating those new varieties falls to a plant breeder: someone who, often painstakingly, crosses plants until they create a new variety. Dr. Jim Myers, one of the most accomplished plant breeders in the country, has lots of experience with this.Myers created the Indigo Rose tomato, a strikingly purple variety with the same antioxidants as blueberries. He also created the green bean cultivar predominantly used by Oregon producers, and is debuting two new varieties of low-heat habanero peppers next month, dubbed “Mild Thing” and “Notta Hotta.”Myers joins Ira Flatow from Corvallis, Oregon, where he’s a professor of agricultural science at Oregon State University. They discuss his decades-long career in plant breeding and what he sees as the biggest challenges for the plant breeders of the future. Subscribe to this podcast. BARBER: So today on the show, what to do when the world's on fire.

#### As the climate changes, is the deadly flooding in Nepal a sign of things to come?

##### Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

It's CONSIDER THIS, where every day we go deep on one big news story. Today, the devastating flooding in Nepal and its links to climate change. Hundreds are dead, and many more are missing after catastrophic flash flooding along the Tibet-Nepal border.

ANDY THAPA: Nothing is visible - no houses, no roads, no any greenery in those areas and no blue water. Now it's muddy water now.

CHANG: Andy Thapa is one of the rescuers trying to get to as many survivors as he can. He's a charter and rescue pilot for a helicopter company in Nepal, and in 20 or so flights over the last two days, he shot some video and shared that video with us.

#### Black Gold - The Future of Food We Throw Away

##### Black Gold: The Future of Food...We Throw Away

![Black Gold: The Future of Food...We Throw Away](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f7e49a04c77574123e5e6fbf5)

**Duration:** 00:51:11

**Released:** 2022

**Series:** Gastropod

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/3F0eADjetCdFyx0j87toeU)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2bB44RWKrgs1jhylH1NBtL)

For a few weeks in 1987, trash was temporarily headline news: a barge filled with waste that would no longer fit in New York City's overflowing landfills spent months wandering up and down the East Coast with nowhere to dump its smelly, rotting cargo. The trash barge's travels triggered a long overdue public rethink of the wisdom of sending all of our waste to landfills—including food. But fast forward more than thirty years, and food still takes up more space in American landfills than anything else. About 30 to 40 percent of food produced in the US gets thrown away, rather than eaten. What's more, putting all that rotting food inside landfills produces a lot of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Our ancestors knew exactly what to do with food waste; the earliest descriptions of composting were written on clay tablets more than 4,000 years ago. So why didn't the GarBarge kick off a composting craze? And why is it so hard for us to keep food waste out of landfills? This episode, Gastropod visits the future of food waste: the high-tech facilities as well as the innovative policies that promise to keep our discarded food out of landfills, keep methane from escaping into the atmosphere, *and* turn those food scraps into something useful. Can a state the size of California really keep 75 percent of its food waste out of landfills, as it has pledged to do by 2025—and what will happen if it does? Listen in for compost blow-dryers, fruit-sticker bingo, and a lot of microbes! Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

:::

#### Catching Fire

![Catching Fire](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f188f54599e90d89a077379e7)

**Duration:** 00:54:43

**Released:** 2024

**Series:** Big Picture Science

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/6jfG9c5PL4njvJVVeZ3XNl)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/0a34nXB83YYHdfDrSSpSkL)

We have too much “bad fire.” Not only destructive wildfires, but the combustion that powers our automobiles and provides our electricity has generated a worrying rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide. And that is driving climate change which is adding to the frequency of megafires. Now we’re seeing those effects in “fire-clouds,” pyrocumulonimbus events. But there’s such a thing as “good fire.” Indigenous peoples managed the land with controlled fires, reaped the benefits of doing so, and they’re bringing them back. So after millions of years of controlling fire, is it time for us to revisit our attitudes and policies, not just with regard to combustion, but how we manage our wildfires? Guests: David Peterson - Meteorologist, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory Stephen Pyne - Emeritus professor at Arizona State University, fire historian, urban farmer, author of “The Pyrocene: How We Created an Age of Fire, and What Happens Next” Richard Wrangham - Ruth B. Moore Research Professor of Biological Anthropology at Harvard University and author of "Catching Fire: How Coooking Made Us Human" Margo Robbins - Co-founder and president of the Cultural Fire Management Council (CFMC), organizer of the Cultural Burn Training Exchange (TREX) that takes place on the Yurok Reservation twice a year, and an enrolled member of the Yurok Tribe Originally aired May 9, 2022 Featuring music by Dewey Dellay and Jun Miyake Big Picture Science is part of the Airwave Media podcast network. Please contact advertising@airwavemedia.com to inquire about advertising on Big Picture Science. This is distinct from excessive unnatural heat, such as a tanning bed death, a little bit of morbid trivia through the morning. Statistical modeling would have expected about fifteen thousand nine hundred and ten deaths based on the previous year, so that gives us an excess of about seven or, five thousand seven hundred. And then the third way of doing this is basically a predictive model. So saying we know when the temperature rises by x amount, this number of people will die and kind of using that model to fit with, the temperatures that were recorded. So there's a bunch of different ways to record excess deaths, a bunch of different models that need to be peer reviewed. And so this this work is still ongoing for heat events, both in Europe and in North America. But this is why you can see many different numbers for how many people died in a given heat wave.

In episode  192 of America Adapts, Doug Parsons hosts Dr. Kelly Turner and Dr. Ladd Keith. Kelly is an Associate Professor of Urban Planning at UCLA and Ladd is an assistant professor in the School of Landscape Architecture and Planning at the University of Arizona.  We learn how extreme heat disproportionately impacts marginalized communities.  We also explore the evolving media coverage of extreme heat. The three of us break down the highs and lows of all the media coverage of extreme heat this past summer.  We also learn about Kelly's research on heat's impact on California schools, and what that means for both public health and student learning.  We take a dive into federal approaches to heat management and learn about the glaring disparity in resources and attention allocated to extreme heat compared to other climate hazards and ponder the potential for FEMA to classify extreme heat as a disaster declaration.  We also discuss the value of having a national adaptation plan for extreme heat planning. Finally, and yes, we go there, we get an update on the efforts to name heat waves. We highlight the pros and cons of this approach and discuss other options.  It is a gangbuster episode and that's just a sampling of what we cover.  Transcripts for this episode available here. (These are computer generated so pardon the errors.)  Topics Covered:    Dr. Turner specializes in heat equity research, while Dr. Keith focuses on heat policy planning and governance.  Increasing prevalence of extreme heat due to climate change and its disproportionate impact on marginalized groups.  Media coverage of extreme heat is becoming more sophisticated, highlighting impacts on workers and public health.  Dr. Turner's research in California focuses on schools and heat's impact on student learning.  Discussion of heating planning strategies including shade in urban design.  The Biden administration is updating heat safety labor laws, emphasizing the need for comprehensive regulations at state and federal levels and the potential for FEMA labeling heat events as disaster declarations.  Naming heat waves to increase public awareness is debated, highlighting the importance of reaching vulnerable populations.  Will heat lead to managed retreat from regions that become uninhabitable?  A national adaptation plan is emphasized to address heat impacts, especially for marginalized communities. #### Designing for climate change

![August 10, 2018: Designing for climate change](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fcd07673e5c5b84f1635010ac)

**Duration:** 00:24:30

**Released:** 2018

**Series:** Better Off

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/7kYJzZ4Eyc2MaqtGxktioK)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

A new study from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health found that students who lived in dormitories without air conditioning during a heat wave performed worse on a series of simple tests compared with students who lived in air-conditioned dorms. The findings show that the effects of extreme heat are not just felt by those typically thought of as vulnerable—such as the elderly. And with global temperatures on the rise, the research underscores the need for sustainable design solutions in mitigating the health impacts of extreme heat. In this week's episode, we'll speak with the authors of that study to learn how we can  better design our buildings and cities to adapt to our changing climate. You'll hear from Joe Allen, assistant professor of exposure assessment science and director of the Healthy Buildings Program at the Center for Climate, Health, and the Global Environment, and Jose Guillermo (Memo) Cedeño Laurent, associate director of the Healthy Buildings Program.

:::

Mosquitoes are the deadliest animal on the planet, and some of them may be on the rise. At least in listener Abigail Krich-Starr's area, that's due to warmer, wetter weather — which, yes, is linked to climate change. But it doesn't stop there: Ecologists and entomologists say increased heat could also alter mosquito behavior, shift their natural habitat, and even change how pathogens incubate and spread inside their bodies.So how do you protect yourself against the (mosquito) masses? Our experts suggested several things:- Assess your risk by checking local mosquito surveillance efforts, like this one for the state of Massachusetts- Consider rescheduling outdoor events happening between dusk and dawn, which is peak biting time for multiple mosquito species- Wear long-sleeved shirts and pants, weather-permitting, to limit exposed skin- Use an EPA-approved DEET repellent, and/or a permethrin spray for clothing and outdoor gearThis episode is part of Nature Quest, a monthly Short Wave segment that answers listener questions about the local environment.Got a question about changes in your local environment? In the Arctic Ocean, sea ice is shrinking as the climate heats up. In the Western U.S., wildfires are getting increasingly destructive. Though discovered relatively recently, Oropouche virus has been making headlines as an emerging vector-borne infectious disease on the rise. Not transmitted by the usual suspects (like ticks and mosquitoes), this virus is instead spread through the bites of midges or no-see-ums. Since these arthropods are already widely distributed and their range is growing thanks to climate change, this is a recipe for potential disaster. In this episode, we take you through the story of Oropouche virus, from how it makes us sick to what the construction of a highway has to do with its discovery, from surprising prevalence statistics to the history of One Health. Tune in for the full scoop on this midge and the virus it carries. #### Smog Cloud Silver Lining

![Smog Cloud Silver Lining](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f9b8e70445903be860a6bdead)

**Duration:** 00:34:28

**Released:** 2023

**Series:** Radiolab

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/7IFXLZbjndycPcrSwHRjkH)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2hmkzUtix0qTqvtpPcMzEL)

Summer 2023 was a pretty scary one for the planet. Global temperatures in June and July reached record highs. And over in the North Atlantic Sea, the water temperature spiked to off-the-chart levels. Some people figured that meant we were about to go over the edge, doomsday. In the face of this, Hank Green (a long time environmentalist and science educator behind SciShow, Crash Course, and more), took to social media to put things in context, to keep people focused on what we can do about climate change. In the process, he came across a couple studies that suggested a reduction in sulfurous smog from cargo ships may have accidentally warmed the waters. And while Hank saw a silver lining around those smog clouds, the story he told—about smog clouds and cooling waters and the problem of geoengineering—took us on a rollercoaster ride of hope and terror. Ultimately, we had to wrestle with the question of what we should be doing about climate change, or what we should even talk about.Special thanks to Dr. Colin Carson and Avishay Artsy. [Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/57R7dOcs60jUfOnuNG0J1R)

On this, our 340th Evolutionary Lens livestream, we discuss the recent flash flood on the border of Nepal and Tibet, climate science, and the nature of evidence. What commonalities are there between a glacial dam breaking and flooding the valley below, taking out towns and villages; Dry Falls and the Columbia River Gorge in Washington state; the Boxing Day tsunami in the Indian Ocean; and the 2011 earthquake that resulted in the destruction of the Fukushima nuclear power plant in Japan? In some cases we have to infer what happened; in some cases we have direct observation; in all cases we have to construct a plausible story that fits all of the evidence. Meanwhile in climate science, a new paper reconstructs NOAA data from 1,200 weather stations from over 100 years, uses a different metric than NOAA does to describe the data, and concludes that the world—or at least the coterminous U.S.—is not heating up in the way we have been told. #### The History And Legacy Of Hurricane Helene

On the night of Sept. 27, 2024, Hurricane Helene dropped a historic wall of rain on the southern Appalachian mountains.Some 31 inches of water fell in three days. The Swannanoa River rose 27 feet. Roads, bridges, and entire communities – very little was left in the storm’s aftermath.  More than 250 people died across the Southeast. More than a hundred of them in North Carolina alone. It was the deadliest hurricane to hit the continental United States since Katrina.We check in on how much western North Carolina has rebuilt in the nearly two years since the storm. Canada is having its worst fire season in modern history. The fires have burnt more than 20 million acres, casting hazardous smoke over parts of the U.S. and stretching Canadian firefighting resources thin. Public officials and many news headlines have declared the fires as "unprecedented," and in the modern-sense they are. But NPR climate correspondent Nate Rott has been talking to researchers who focus on the history of wildfire in Canada's boreal forests and they say the situation is not without precedent.Want more stories on the environment? #### Ticks are a growing problem, no matter where you live

![Ticks are a growing problem, no matter where you live](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fd6dfd33952fcc32f38efadc1)

**Duration:** 00:13:14

**Released:** 2026

**Series:** Short Wave

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5m5WghWyi9qJIZcvJej9cs)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2rTT1klKUoQNuaW2Ah19Pa)

In the grand scheme of things, Lyme disease is a fairly new scientific discovery. It was first traced back to ticks in the late 70s and early 80s. The tick-borne illness can cause a rash, fever, pain, neurological complications, and even facial paralysis. It’s spread by only two of the nearly 50 species of ticks in the United States. Historically, most Lyme cases were limited to a small region, including the Great Lakes area and northeastern US. But thanks to changing temperatures, animal migration and shifts in land use, scientists say tick territory is expanding. So what does that mean for Lyme disease risk? And do you have to be worried about it in your own backyard?Interested in more episodes about pests and parasites? #### What Ever Happened to the Ozone Hole?

![What Ever Happened to the Ozone Hole?](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fdcb86b6f8a4a93e27259d570)

**Duration:** 00:39:21

**Released:** 2026

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/5zO1JRIY0pon3rxHEEbm8X)

A dark blue wound across the bottom of the world — that’s what NASA images showed in the 1980s. It was a hole in the ozone layer, eight million square miles across. Human activity and convenience had quietly, but rapidly, eaten away  Earth’s crucial shield against the sun, one that likely helped make life on land possible in the first place.Ben Bradford goes back to re-examine the story of the ozone hole: how people discovered it, how they fought over what to do, and what finally happened. It’s a tale of hairspray, human progress, exploding refrigerators, scientists balancing on icy Antarctic rooftops, and Ronald Reagan’s ranch. And from it, maybe, we can find a map for building consensus on our most pressing environmental challenges today.Guest:Susan Solomon, MIT atmospheric scientist and one of the key figures in solving the ozone crisis.Support Are We Doomed?, get bonus episodes, and more: https://doompod.com/support/ Watch earlier episodes on Youtube! https://www.youtube.com/@arewedoomedpod  To manage podcast ad preferences, review the links below:See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for sponsorship and to manage your podcast sponsorship preferences. #### What we lose if the Great Salt Lake dries up

![What we lose if the Great Salt Lake dries up](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fe30d347bbe3d0462f72b1c86)

**Duration:** 00:12:31

**Released:** 2023

**Series:** Short Wave

<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/1164829382/1200392913" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"></iframe>

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1fd8eq7653xN4mr4D29EWD)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2rTT1klKUoQNuaW2Ah19Pa)

Dotted across the Great Basin of the American West are salty, smelly lakes. The largest of these, by far, is the Great Salt Lake in Utah.But a recent report found that water diversions for farming, climate change and population growth could mean the lake essentially disappears within five years. Less water going in means higher concentrations of salt and minerals, which threatens the crucial ecological role saline lakes play across the West, as well as the health of the people who live nearby. On today's episode, Kirk takes Short Wave co-host Aaron Scott on an audio field trip to the endangered Great Salt Lake, and explains why losing the lake could be devastating for everyone from brine flies to the humans that live next door. #### What Worsening Floods Mean For Superfund Sites

![What Worsening Floods Mean For Superfund Sites](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f90d89c0fe8a494a3a4d55c49)

**Duration:** 00:17:52

**Released:** 2024

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/529FSErk9SjroIvEiJ0NVA)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/5UpA5Uw23B6bukC0TABffC)

Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Floodwaters can move toxic waste into neighboring communities, which threatens drinking water, agriculture, and broader ecosystem health.Read more at sciencefriday.comTranscripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. **0:02** · COMMISSIONER GREGG BISHOP: The "urban heat island" effect affects a lot of cities like New York. Because a tremendous amount of buildings, a lot of concrete, and little vegetation increases the overall temperature of the city. And when the city is really, really, really hot, it affects the health of our citizens, individuals who may suffer from asthma, or may be susceptible to heat waves, our elderly population. So, heat actually affects life and safety.

**0:31** · One of the strategies that we have to combat the urban heat island effect is the NYC CoolRoofs initiative, which works simply by painting the roofs white.

**0:39** · BRIDGET CARTER: See how the coating is going inside the seams?

**0:42** · Put it on as heavy as you can get it.

**0:44** · BISHOP: Many buildings, because of the black roof, absorb heat. And painting them white reduces the internal temperature of a building by 10-30 percent.

**0:53** · CARTER: Remember guys, don't stretch the coating.

**0:55** · Don't stretch the coating.

**0:56** · Where is your bucket?

**0:57** · That reflective coating is going to keep the building cooler, conserve energy for the people that live in the building— less air conditioning and less fans being run. People can save some money.

**1:07** · Very energy efficient.

**1:08** · BISHOP: This CoolRoofs program is really a part of the Mayor's strategy to lower New York City's emissions by 80 percent by 2050, and to really help New York City become a great partner in fighting climate change.

#### Drowning in seaweed How to stop invasive Sargassum

**nature video**, *01 25, 2023*

##### Video (10:31)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/CH7MpiGCdgU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The story of Sargassum stretches from the Congo to the Amazon, from soybean farming to climate change and from toxic gases to robotic vehicles. In this documentary researchers from around the world explain the vast scope of the Sargassum problem and the solutions that may one day begin to address it.

Additional photographs and footage in this film were provided by Drake Lee-Patterson, Gary Marshall, Joseph Weekes, Driven Visual Media, Kerwin Noel,  Nick Hurley, Akeisha Clark, Sargassum Information Hub, NASA, Chuanmin Hu, Jeff Davis's team, Hazel Oxenford, Caroline Juang, Melvina Walsh, Morgan Lewis, Kerton Jobe, P McConney, Markel Gomez Letona and Nico Frohberg who were mistakenly missed off the film credits.

**0:03** · VOICE OVER: The Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt is the largest seaweed bloom in the world, and it's expanding.

**0:11** · Visible from space, it's a growing problem for coastal communities.

**0:15** · HARSHINI VUMMADI: The beaches, genuinely, if they aren't maintained, you just can't go there.

**0:21** · You'd be up to your knees in sargassum.

**0:24** · VOICE OVER: But as a key sequester of carbon, this invasive species also presents an opportunity.

**0:30** · AJIT SUBRAMANIAM: We want to gather sargassum using robotic vehicles.

**0:34** · You sink it down 2,000 metres, our current model suggests that that particular water body does not come back in contact with the atmosphere for at least 100 years.

**0:42** · VOICE OVER: Can scientists take a global challenge and turn it into an opportunity to buy time in the race against climate change?

**1:00** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum has been in the Atlantic since the time of Christopher Columbus, floating mats of seaweed that gave its name to the Sargasso Sea – a nutrient-poor patch of the Atlantic penned in by ocean currents.

**1:13** · AJIT: You can think of it as a floating rainforest or an upside-down coral reef because each raft of sargassum is a hotspot of biological activity.

**1:22** · VOICE OVER: But in the last couple of decades, a new population has emerged, further south near the coast of Brazil and the Caribbean.

**1:29** · SHELLY-ANN COX: In 2011, we were all taken back by this new phenomenon, where we saw tons of sargassum being brought and beached in the region.

**1:42** · VOICE OVER: Based in Barbados, scientist and entrepreneur Shelly-Ann Cox specialises in fisheries management.

**1:49** · She first noticed the impact of sargassum on the sea urchin divers she was working with.

**1:54** · SHELLY-ANN: Fisher folk had reported sargassum mats as far as their eyes can see.

**2:01** · Some of them can't get to the boat or the boats can't get through the sargassum to get out.

**2:07** · Those near shore, the spear fishers as well, they reported some of their skin being irritated when they're diving and the berries that keep the sargassum floating have gotten into their ears as well.

**2:21** · VOICE OVER: The impact on tourism – the lifeblood of the Caribbean – has been huge.

**2:25** · OFF-SCREEN VOICE: This weed is going right up to the sanitation plant by Barnacle Point.

**2:33** · People, get ready for the smell tomorrow.

**2:39** · VOICE OVER: Around the same time, other scientists working in the Atlantic had also noticed a change.

**2:45** · Oceanographer Ajit Subramaniam has been working in the South Atlantic for more than 25 years.

**2:50** · AJIT: In 2018, it was astounding how much sargassum we ran into, and it was really striking.

**2:55** · It was something that we'd never seen before and then, bam.

**2:58** · We were there, and the ship was often surrounded by sargassum that was hundreds of metres around the ship.

**3:05** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum wasn't thought to be found this far south.

**3:08** · AJIT: We were seeing things that we had not seen before, and I was trying to get context for that.

**3:12** · VOICE OVER: Ajit linked up with colleagues at the University of South Florida, who had been making their own observations.

**3:17** · AJIT: They'd been actually watching this on their satellite data, and they had actually seen this explosion of this new population that is growing much closer to the equator.

**3:26** · VOICE OVER: With the satellite data, scientists were able to hazard an estimate of its size.

**3:31** · SHELLY-ANN: 24.2 million metric tons in June, from the satellite imagery.

**3:38** · VOICE OVER: Dubbed the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt, this is almost certainly the world's largest macroalgal bloom.

**3:44** · It's thought that intensive agriculture, especially soya plantations, has increased nitrogen concentrations in the Atlantic, causing rapid sargassum growth.

**3:54** · SHELLY-ANN: Sargassum is really known as a symptom of climate change because, due to increasing surface temperatures, nutrients from the Amazon and Congo, Saharan dust which brings in iron, upwelling as well, the change in currents, all of these factors have led to the proliferation of sargassum.

**4:19** · HARSHINI: Outside of the Caribbean, I don't think many people are talking about this.

**4:23** · VOICE OVER: Harshini Vummadi is a biology major undergraduate, who's recently returned from an exploratory trip to the Dominican Republic.

**4:32** · HARSHINI: It affects the Caribbean and I believe West Africa, and a bit of East Asia as well.

**4:40** · VOICE OVER: Harshini is part of an interdisciplinary team from the Georgia Institute of Technology.

**4:44** · They're working with the school of biological sciences to try and explore solutions to the sargassum problem.

**4:49** · RESEARCHER: Yeah, so, I'm just collecting some sargassum samples and there are lots of different plants in here.

**4:57** · HARSHINI: I am the biology major on their team. We have a chemical engineer, a civil engineer, a mechanical engineer.

**5:03** · VOICE OVER: A solution of some sort is definitely needed, and urgently.

**5:07** · HARSHINI: I just didn't realise how much of it there would be, like we watched a clean-up crew work and work, and in 2 hours they like hardly made a dent. The growth just seems to be almost exponential.

**5:18** · VOICE OVER: While there are many creative small-scale craft uses of sargassum, local communities have yet to find a viable solution to disposing of vast quantities of the stuff, or even better, making it useful.

**5:30** · HARSHINI: It uptakes a lot of different heavy metals, particularly arsenic, which makes it like quite dangerous to use as, say, like a fertiliser because, again, now you're introducing arsenic to these land systems where it could potentially leach into groundwater.

**5:47** · So, we try to like branch out from fertiliser. One of our team members focused on an application involving bricks.

**5:55** · Someone else focused on black soldier fly larvae, which could consume the sargassum and then in turn be used as a sort of biofuel in like an anaerobic digester.

**6:08** · I personally have been working on using it as a bioaccumulate. Why not use it in waste water treatment?

**6:16** · It can absorb those heavy metals that we were so concerned about in the first place.

**6:21** · VOICE OVER: Harshini's team are working on ways to make the sargassum financially viable.

**6:26** · Meanwhile, Ajit is thinking more broadly, exploring the bigger checks and balances of the global carbon cycle.

**6:32** · He's come up with a radical plan.

**6:34** · AJIT: So, the way we want to do this is essentially gather nets of sargassum using robotic vehicles, have them ballasted and then sink them down to 2,000 metres.

**6:46** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum sequesters a lot of carbon, but it also releases it when it decays.

**6:52** · This approach would theoretically remove the carbon from the atmosphere, effectively buying the planet time in the race against climate change.

**6:59** · AJIT: Sinking down 2,000 metres, our current model suggests that that particular water body does not come back in contact with the atmosphere for at least 100 years.

**7:08** · VOICE OVER: The idea of sinking the sargassum has been proposed before, but the suggestion is usually to sink it where it grows, in shallower water.

**7:15** · AJIT: Merely capturing it at the surface and getting rid of it just off the beach at 100 metres or something like that will basically have the carbon coming right back up.

**7:26** · It might even actually come back up in a more potent form if you are starting to have it rotting and forming methane.

**7:32** · VOICE OVER: Ajit plans to sink the sargassum in deeper water, but there are a lot of questions still to be answered.

**7:38** · AJIT: We want to make sure that the carbon that we are capturing is actually going down to the sea floor and will stay down there, and so we want to follow it down to the sea floor.

**7:46** · VOICE OVER: In addition, as a biologist, he's keen to understand the impact of this plan on the ecosystem.

**7:51** · AJIT: So, we actually have a fisheries scientist on the team who will be looking at what kind of communities the sargassum rafts harbour, and therefore we'll have a sense of what we might be impacting if we were to do the sinking.

**8:02** · It's not that we're going to decimate the ocean of sargassum.

**8:06** · VOICE OVER: The list of problems attributed to sargassum is growing. From the harmful gases released when it decays to its impact on wildlife.

**8:13** · HARSHINI: Especially when it washes up on beaches where turtles go to lay their eggs, a lot of these baby turtles are actually unable to climb over these sargassum things, and so they're unable to make it into the ocean due to these big patches of sargassum.

**8:28** · SHELLY-ANN: So, every year we're seeing more countries reporting the influx and the catastrophic impacts on tourism, fisheries sectors, maritime and transport and then the health impacts.

**8:43** · So, some of our colleagues recently published a paper on the impacts on pregnant women who were exposed to hydrogen sulfide and ammonia when the sargassum decomposes.

**8:57** · Those pregnant ladies who live near the coast and were exposed were at a higher risk of preeclampsia.

**9:04** · VOICE OVER: Going into the future, it's likely that the challenge presented by sargassum, like many of the challenges of climate change, might be bigger than one scientist or one idea.

**9:14** · HARSHINI: There needs to be some sort of economically driven, or at least be governmentally subsidised, but there needs to be some sort of way to like tackle and solve the problem.

**9:27** · AJIT: I feel that countries like Barbados are the populations that contribute the least to climate change and yet are facing the greatest impact of climate change.

**9:36** · I would like to figure out a financing model where we can actually have credit going to communities in Barbados for the carbon that is sequestered.

**9:46** · SHELLY-ANN: There are lots of bright, brilliant minds out there developing solutions that need this support.

**9:53** · They need the financial support to upscale until governments realise that this problem is really here to stay, then they will be willing then to invest in building up sargassum industries.

**10:07** · HARSHINI: Nothing has like had any concrete potential yet. There's just several isolated research groups.

**10:15** · But I just think that things would move a lot faster if everyone could like work together.

#### Extreme Heat Is the New Normal

**New York Times Opinion**, *08 28, 2026*

##### Video (15:42)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/QcHuAtK_H_8 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.

In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.

Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.

With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

Documentary and text by By Nita Blum-Reddick and Jonathan Pickett

##### Description

Humans are increasingly reliant on air conditioning, but its use contributes to global warming. As the world warms and demand rises, how can we make A/C sustainable? In Spain and India, Kal Penn explores two innovative solutions. 

---
Getting Warmer is Bloomberg's exclusive new show about climate, clean energy and business, anchored by actor and former White House aide Kal Penn.

Accompany him on his journey as he takes an up-close look at bold climate solutions and discovers new facets of the global transition to clean energy.

In a hosted studio segment, Penn sifts through the overwhelming news about our climate and breaks down the facts and trends to understand with a dose of humor and optimism. Why are the recycling symbols on your plastic cups misleading? How does the carbon credit market work and does it actually help? And what is the future of water in a drought-ridden world?

On the road, Penn meets the innovators, researchers, communities and businesses pivoting to new energy sources and spearheading low-carbon technologies. In documentary segments, Penn speaks to the self-declared “crypto cowboys” of Texas who claim Bitcoin mining can help stabilize the state’s troubled electrical grid, and travels to Nevada to visit the company attempting to build America’s first closed-loop supply chain for electric vehicles. In New York, Penn explores the urban designs proposed to save the city from the next Superstorm Sandy and goes inside New York’s Empire State building to investigate the challenges of decarbonizing our cities and landmarks. 

The show builds on, and includes contributions from, Bloomberg Green’s award-winning team of climate journalists as well as London-based climate storytellers Jack Harries and Alice Aedy. With a focus on the most pressing questions for young viewers, Jack and Alice unpack one big idea each episode. From recycled wastewater to regenerative agriculture and the challenges of a just transition for workers in the energy sector, they’ll break down how countries across the world are finding intriguing solutions to our climate crisis, and outline the challenges ahead.

#### How America's hottest city is trying to cool down

**Vox**, *09 20, 2021*

##### Video (6:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/ZQ6fSHr5TJg title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?

Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don't miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them. 

Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 
1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 
2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. 
And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable. 

As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located. 

So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down. 

This is the first video of five videos we're releasing on climate change. You can watch the second video, about high-voltage transmission lines ⚡️ and why the US isn't ready for clean energy, here: https://youtu.be/s3ScJ_FwaZk

And the third video dives into prescribed burns, and how a decade of suppressing forest fires 🔥  may have made them worse, here: https://youtu.be/0o6ezu_h6iE

Right here, on the heels of the Lahaina disaster and a summer full of Canadian wildfire smoke, we’ve been wondering: when the air fills with smoke, what are you really breathing? How best to protect yourself? And how bad is it going to get? 

Along with Alok, Maiya May from Weathered brings some long-term perspective on fires, climate change and the shifting patterns of where we live.

##### Description

These "sponge city" designs resist floods and increase biodiversity to help us adapt to a changing climate.

This episode is presented by Delta. Delta doesn’t have a say in our editorial decisions, but they make videos like this possible. For more information, visit http://www.delta.com/sustainability.

Subscribe to our channel and turn on notifications (🔔) so you don't miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

From rising sea levels in Mumbai to unbearable heat in Houston, cities around the world are feeling the effects of climate change. Unfortunately, they don’t always have the right infrastructure to handle its impacts — which is one reason why cities are beginning to reimagine urban design. One of these designs is a “sponge city.”

Although one city design certainly won’t save us from the effects of climate change, “sponge cities” can help with how we live with it. 

Here are some studies and articles we used to inform our reporting:

Biodiversity — our strongest natural defense against climate change: https://www.un.org/en/climatechange/science/climate-issues/biodiversity

Sponge City, Shenzhen Explores the Benefits of Designing with Nature: https://www.lincolninst.edu/publications/articles/sponge-city-shenzhen-explores-benefits-designing-with-nature

Sponge City Practices in China: From Pilot Exploration to Systemic Demonstration: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/14/10/1531

The ocean is rising — and so is Miami’s skyline: https://www.vox.com/climate/23872640/coastal-climate-ocean-rising-miami-florida-building

Sponge Cities: Integrating Green and Gray Infrastructure to Build Climate Change Resilience in the People’s Republic of China: https://www.adb.org/sites/default/files/publication/838386/adb-brief-222-sponge-cities-prc.pdf

How Is Climate Change Affecting Floods?: https://www.nytimes.com/article/flooding-climate-change.html

The Colorado River is running out — and the Imperial Valley is ground zero. As policymakers battle over rights to a shrinking river, farmers are grappling with the practical realities of growing food with less water. Miles O’Brien meets two Imperial Valley farmers who are finding ways to feed people and livestock, nearby and abroad, while trying to make good use of every drop of this hard-working river.

###### Intro

**0:01** · If you look at a thermal image of a city and then compare that to a map of vegetation, you'll find that where there's greenery, the temperature is lower.

**0:11** · That's because things like asphalt, concrete and shingled roofs absorb more heat from the sun than trees.

**0:19** · This is the urban heat island effect, and it accounts for the higher temperatures in cities, often by several degrees compared with their surroundings.

**0:28** · It's becoming a huge risk to human health as growing urban populations exacerbate the heating effects of climate change.

**0:36** · Heat waves kill more people than any other extreme weather event, more than tornadoes, hurricanes and even floods.

**0:47** · That's why urban heat island mitigation strategies are being studied in Singapore by a group of researchers.

**0:54** · The government-backed project called Cooling Singapore is now in the process of combining everything they've learned to create a digital tool that can help cities all over the world, starting with Singapore.

###### Cooling Singapore

**1:10** · In Singapore, close to the equator, temperatures regularly rise above 32 degrees Celsius or 90 degrees Fahrenheit.

**1:19** · And the city structures only make it worse.

**1:22** · And that is also the case for Singapore, which is basically a concrete jungle, more urbanized, more developed city.

**1:29** · And even in Singapore, what you have is a situation whereby there's a temperature difference of 7 degrees Celsius between the more urbanized and the more rural areas.

**1:41** · The government has taken drastic steps to keep temperatures down.

**1:46** · This is Gardens by the Bay, an award-winning park.

**1:50** · And inside this greenhouse it's a pleasant 24 degrees.

**1:54** · That's because the dome, along with two dozen nearby towers full of thousands of people, is chilled by what's probably the world's largest underground district cooling system.

**2:04** · It uses a large central plant that cools water and then pipes it into banks, residential towers, an exhibition center, shopping malls and the city's iconic Marina Bay Sands hotel and casino complex.

**2:18** · So one of the biggest perks of using this system for the buildings is that they can save 40% in terms of electricity usage compared to your traditional air conditioners.

**2:32** · And with Singapore relying on natural gas for most of its power, this new system means emissions savings equivalent to removing 10,000 cars from the city's roads.

**2:43** · That has big implications for the rest of the world.

**2:45** · If things stay as they are, more than a third of the world's electricity could end up being used to cool buildings and vehicles by 2050.

**2:55** · As the world gets hotter, gets warmer, there is a greater need for air conditioning and as well as refrigerators, for instance.

**3:03** · And the more people are buying these household appliances, the more energy usage they use and they release heat more, and that then exacerbates climate change.

**3:18** · It's a vicious circle.

###### Vegetation

**3:20** · And so since 2017, researchers at Cooling Singapore have been identifying design solutions that reduce our need for so much cool air in the first place.

**3:31** · One thing many cities have in common, and that's the importance of vegetation.

**3:36** · That's a very important measure to mitigate the urban heat because of the shading effect, of course, and deep psychological effects of the vegetation.

**3:46** · And also because of the possible evaporative cooling effect of the vegetation.

**3:53** · Vegetation can be, of course, on the ground floor in form of trees and shrubs.

**3:58** · And you can walk under them.

**4:00** · This is the so-called canopy layer that the vegetation forms above us.

**4:05** · But vegetation can also go up the facades of buildings and it can go to the roof of the buildings.

###### Garden City Feel

**4:14** · Luckily, Singapore has been striving for the Garden City feel for quite some time.

**4:20** · It was a vision initially introduced by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in 1967 to make life more pleasant for people.

**4:28** · And today, Singapore is one of the world's greenest cities in terms of urban vegetation.

**4:33** · Kampung Admiralty, a community center that contains health facilities and social spaces, now provides more green space than the plot of land it was originally built on.

**4:44** · It's topped by a roofscape of staggered terraces covered in local plants, which functions as a community park, and a village green in the center that contains farm plots for residents to tend to.

**4:56** · Parkroyal on Pickering was designed as a hotel in a garden that doubled the green-growing potential of its site.

**5:04** · There's now 15,000 meters of sky gardens, reflecting pools, waterfalls, planter terraces and green walls.

**5:12** · And the government has big plans as well.

**5:17** · Singapore actually has a plan to plant 1 million trees and add more green spaces over the next 10 years.

**5:24** · It is actually a mix of one thing to reduce the urban heat island effect.

**5:30** · But on the other hand, it's also to to get the people to be more connected to nature.

**5:39** · But it's not enough.

###### Heat Mitigation

**5:41** · The city-state has still been warming twice as quickly as the world average over the past six decades.

**5:47** · That's why Cooling Singapore has developed a catalog of other potential heat-mitigation measures.

**5:54** · When you try to mitigate the urban heat island effect in a city or in any building, in a village as well, the first place to start is by shading of the windows.

**6:05** · You have to keep areas clear so that the wind can move through it.

**6:11** · Water of a certain depth can act as a very good thermal buffer.

**6:15** · If you have to construct heavy buildings, such as high rises, at least you can make the surface, the facade less heavy.

**6:24** · And you can protect it from direct sun penetration.

**6:27** · We have to make sure that no combustion engines will be in the city in the middle, in the medium- to long-term range.

**6:35** · So ideally, the electricity production is outside of the city.

**6:39** · And you bring just the clean electricity into the city.

**6:43** · You can at least minimize the use of energy in the city.

**6:48** · And you can start to slowly convert the roofs, the facades of the city, into production areas for renewable energy.

**6:58** · In Singapore, unfortunately, this is a limited option.

**7:01** · But in the long run, it could produce up to 20%, 25% of the energy, of the electricity needed in Singapore.

**7:10** · If all the roofs and the areas in the buildings, on the buildings, on the facades would be used to do that.

###### Urban Climate Twin

**7:20** · With so many different ideas, Cooling Singapore is also designing a virtual model of the city to test them out.

**7:26** · It's called a Digital Urban Climate Twin, or DUCT, that will calculate how each element of the city's design will impact the urban heat island effect.

**7:37** · That means we model not only the geometry of the buildings digitally, but also we model the transportation, the insulation, the temperature, the radiation coming from the sun, the weather, the local weather, the local climate, the even very, very microclimate of the city, the water, the movement of people in the city.

**8:01** · We can invent scenarios.

**8:04** · We can design scenarios, test them before we actually build them.

**8:09** · And if they test very well and we are sure that they will function, then we can start to build them and put them into reality.

###### Conclusion

**8:23** · Singapore will be using this new tool to figure out which actions it should take next.

**8:28** · And the model can be applied to any city, whether it needs to keep heat out or keep heat in, which will ultimately save energy, slow climate change and improve our quality of life.

**8:41** · So this is something that Singapore will be able to export, maybe even together with its city development systems that it already has.

**8:51** · Singapore is one of the very few cities in the world that really combined this scientific approach with a very well-established urban redesign and urban design approach.

**9:03** · Through its agencies and the combination of its agencies, it has achieved a lot in the past.

**9:10** · If it keeps following the scientific path and the combination with the other knowledge in the city already, we think that it will be a very comfortable and very livable city in the future, even more than today.

Check out our Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/cw/PBSWeathered?utm_medium=unknown&utm_source=join_link&utm_campaign=creatorshare_creator&utm_content=copyLink 

Fires are getting bigger and more homes are burning each year. In January 2025, 14 out of control wildfires tore through parts of Los Angeles and burnt over 18,000 structures and left at least 29 people dead. Firefighters are having to change tactics when it comes to the most destructive fires, but why? Jennifer Blach, Ph.D., just released a new study in the journal, Science, and her findings point to a new type of fire that is the culprit for all this destruction. 

In this episode, we dive into this groundbreaking new study to learn why fires are getting more dangerous to humans and what we can do about it. Plus we have never-before-seen animations from NASA that show us exactly how these new fires behave. So tune in to learn about the future of fires and how to protect yourself and your home as fires change.

#### Urbanization and the future of cities - Vance Kite

**TED-Ed**, *09 12, 2013*

##### Video (4:08)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/fKnAJCSGSdk title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

View full lesson: http://ed.ted.com/lessons/urbanization-and-the-future-of-cities-vance-kite

About 10,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers, aided by rudimentary agriculture, moved to semi-permanent villages and never looked back. With further developments came food surpluses, leading to commerce, specialization and, many years later with the Industrial Revolution, the modern city. Vance Kite plots our urban past and how we can expect future cities to adapt to our growing populations. 

Lesson by Vance Kite, animation by ATMG Studio.

##### Transcript

**0:06** · Today ,more than half of all people in the world live in an urban area.

**0:11** · By mid-century, this will increase to 70%.

**0:14** · But as recently as 100 years ago, only two out of ten people lived in a city, and before that, it was even less.

**0:21** · How have we reached such a high degree of urbanization, and what does it mean for our future?

**0:27** · In the earliest days of human history, humans were hunter-gatherers, often moving from place to place in search of food.

**0:35** · But about 10,000 years ago, our ancestors began to learn the secrets of selective breeding and early agricultural techniques.

**0:42** · For the first time, people could raise food rather than search for it, and this led to the development of semi-permanent villages for the first time in history.

**0:51** · "Why only semi-permanent?" you might ask.

**0:54** · Well, at first, the villages still had to relocate every few years as the soil became depleted.

**1:00** · It was only with the advent of techniques like irrigation and soil tilling about 5,000 years ago that people could rely on a steady and long-term supply of food, making permanent settlements possible.

**1:11** · And with the food surpluses that these techniques produced, it was no longer necessary for everyone to farm.

**1:17** · This allowed the development of other specialized trades, and, by extension, cities.

**1:23** · With cities now producing surplus food, as well as tools, crafts, and other goods, there was now the possibility of commerce and interaction over longer distances.

**1:33** · And as trade flourished, so did technologies that facilitated it, like carts, ships, roads, and ports.

**1:43** · Of course, these things required even more labor to build and maintain, so more people were drawn from the countryside to the cities as more jobs and opportunities became available.

**1:52** · If you think modern cities are overcrowded, you may be surprised to learn that some cities in 2000 B.C. had population densities nearly twice as high as that of Shanghai or Calcutta.

**2:03** · One reason for this was that transportation was not widely available, so everything had to be within walking distance, including the few sources of clean water that existed then.

**2:13** · And the land area of the city was further restricted by the need for walls to defend against attacks.

**2:20** · The Roman Empire was able to develop infrastructure to overcome these limitations, but other than that, modern cities as we know them, didn't really get their start until the Industrial Revolution, when new technology deployed on a mass scale allowed cities to expand and integrate further, establishing police, fire, and sanitation departments, as well as road networks, and later electricity distribution.

###### Industrial Revolution


###### What Is the Future of Cities

**2:43** · So, what is the future of cities?

**2:46** · Global population is currently more than 7 billion and is predicted to top out around 10 billion.

**2:52** · Most of this growth will occur in the urban areas of the world's poorest countries.

**2:57** · So, how will cities need to change to accommodate this growth?

**3:01** · First, the world will need to seek ways to provide adequate food, sanitation, and education for all people.

**3:07** · Second, growth will need to happen in a way that does not damage the land that provides us with the goods and services that support the human population.

**3:17** · Food production might move to vertical farms and skyscrapers, rooftop gardens, or vacant lots in city centers, while power will increasingly come from multiple sources of renewable energy.

**3:28** · Instead of single-family homes, more residences will be built vertically.

**3:33** · We may see buildings that contain everything that people need for their daily life, as well as a smaller, self-sufficient cities focused on local and sustainable production.

###### The Future of Cities

**3:42** · The future of cities is diverse, malleable, and creative, no longer built around a single industry, but reflecting an increasingly connected and global world.

#### What Does Extreme Heat Do to the Body

**PBS**, *09 03, 2026*

##### Video (9:59)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/wXoqEJlsKu0?start=2 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Watch more of this series: https://to.pbs.org/4wkQIAG

The climate crisis isn't a distant threat — it's already here, and it's deadly. But keeping people cool is surprisingly complicated. 

In Sydney, Australia, physiologist Ollie Jay is tackling the problem by studying how the human body responds to extreme heat. The ultimate goal is to create low-cost cooling strategies for people without access to air conditioning — those most at risk from extreme heat. Science journalist Miles O'Brien puts himself in the hot seat — literally — to find out what it feels like when the body's cooling system starts to fail.

Heat is the deadliest weather hazard in the U.S. and many places around the world, and it's only getting worse.

The most deadly heat waves so far have been dry heat waves. But a new threat is rising: humid heat waves, aka wet-bulb events. Scientists have identified wet-bulb temperatures where sweat can’t evaporate fast enough to cool the human body. And once this threshold is crossed, it doesn’t matter how much shade or water you have: you won’t survive without environmental cooling like air conditioning.

In this episode of Weathered, we break down: What wet-bulb temperature actually means, why it’s so dangerous, what areas will be affected, and why air conditioning, while essential, isn’t enough.

###### Air pollution

**0:35** · Cities are centers of industry, but the resulting pollution is filling our lungs and making us sick.

**0:41** · One major culprit is particulate matter: airborne particles of dust, soot and smoke that are released when we burn fossil fuels or kicked up during construction and farming.

**0:49** · When we inhale them, they can cause asthma and they can also enter our bloodstream to cause strokes and even death.

**0:54** · Experts estimate that outdoor air pollution kills over three million people a year and as cities grow, leaders are funding creative—and often expensive—solutions for the problem.

**1:04** · In London, the mayor spent over a million pounds spraying city streets with an adhesive that was supposed to glue pollutants to the road.

**1:10** · and in the Netherlands, designers have created a giant air purifier they call "The Smog Free Tower", which is cool, but there is another, simpler solution… A new report from The Nature Conservancy shows that planting trees can be a cost-effective way to improve public health, which they do in two ways: First, a tree removes particulate matter when polluted air blows through its branches.

###### Planting trees

**1:31** · The particulate matter settles on the leaves and when it rains the dust is washed down the gutter so we don’t inhale it.

**1:37** · Second, trees cool temperatures by providing shade and releasing water through photosynthesis, which cools summer temperatures by about two to four degrees fahrenheit.

**1:46** · But there is a catch!

**1:47** · Trees can only clean and cool the air within a close radius: about one hundred feet, so city officials need to be careful where they plant.

**1:54** · Officials can maximize pollution reduction by planting trees where population density and air pollution overlap.

**1:59** · The Nature Conservancy report uses data from Washington D.C. to create a map showing where planting trees will have the highest return on investment.

**2:06** · And some trees work better than others: trees with larger, stickier leaves, like maples and elms are more effective, but they also need to be considered within the larger ecosystem.

**2:15** · Compared to DC, many cities around the world have even more to gain from planting trees: this map shows where return on investment is highest for reducing particulate matter.

**2:23** · With proper targeting, planting trees can be just as cost-effective as other strategies like converting public transportation to use less diesel fuel.

**2:30** · But there is one major limiting factor: water access.

**2:34** · What might work in Boston, will be less feasible in a city like Doha, Qatar, where water is a scarce resource.

**2:39** · And on top of that, many mayors don’t yet think of trees as a public health resource.

**2:44** · Trees might not look like giant air filters, but that’s exactly what they are, and the sooner we start thinking of them that way, the sooner the air we breathe might be cooler and cleaner in cities around the world.

###### The Heat Island Effect

**0:24** · All of that asphalt, concrete, dark rooftops and tall buildings— they absorb and store heat.

**0:31** · And there are a lot of people using a lot of energy— driving cars, riding subways, running the AC.

**0:38** · All of these materials and activities either create or retain heat.

**0:44** · And all that stored heat causes steeper nighttime highs … when people would otherwise have a chance to cool down.

**0:52** · The way all these heat-storing elements are laid out matters quite a bit.

**0:57** · In cities laid out in grids, like Phoenix, Chicago, or Washington, D.C., the buildings are closer together, like closely packed coals in a fire, keeping heat in.

**1:07** · More space between buildings creates more circulation.

**1:11** · Another way to combat this heat island effect is through green space.

**1:15** · Parks, trees, plants— they don’t absorb as much heat … they actually send water back in the atmosphere.

Filmed during the hottest days of Phoenix, Arizona’s summer heatwave, A NEW INFERNO follows paramedics as they race to save the lives of heatstroke victims using a radical new treatment: ice immersion therapy.  As featured on the NY Times Op Docs — We Are Living in a New Inferno  World Premiere SXSW Film Festival, 2026  Featuring Jason Smith, Jake West, Roy Lewis, & Colter Fosdick Directed & Produced by Nita Blum-Reddick & Jonathan Pickett Executive Producers Sam Osborn, Alejandra Vasquez, & Jesse Ray Sheps Cinematographer Ryan Dent  Editor Jonathan Pickett  Composer Jack Gillette Production Sound Mixer Daniel Reddick  Grips Stephane Strande & Brian Osback Sound Design & Mix Hansdale Hsu Colorist Keyhan Bayegan Production Assistant Camden Smith Title & Poster Designer Jason Cryer Weather Consultant Jorge Torres Advisors Dr. Charles Finch, Medical Director, Phoenix Fire Department & Maki Lloyd, Deputy Chief, Phoenix Fire Department  For The New York Times Op-Docs: Associate Producers Ingrid Homquist & Rebecca Shaid Producer Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo Senior Producer Andrew Blackwell Executive Producer Alexandra Garcia  Please consider supporting the ongoing work of Circle the City: www.circlethecity.org  Festivals: • Tribeca x NYT Op-Docs • Mountainfilm • Rooftop Films • Palm Springs International ShortFest • Indy Shorts Film Festival • HollyShorts Film Festival • Nashville Film Festival • Bend Film Festival • Mill Valley Film Festival • Sidewalk Film Festival • deadCenter Film Festival • Ouray International Film Festival • Cinema Columbus • AfterImage Film Festival • Coast Film Festival

##### Description

Check out our Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/cw/PBSWeathered?utm_medium=unknown&utm_source=join_link&utm_campaign=creatorshare_creator&utm_content=copyLink 

It is WILD how often cities used to burn down. So when fires ripped through LA at the beginning of 2025, we wondered: are urban firestorms BACK? 

In 1871, nearly a third of Chicago burned down. In 1889, 25 blocks of Seattle went up in flames. Modern buildings and firefighting solved the problem. So, how is this happening again? And why is it getting worse? To find out, we went to LA while the fires were still burning. Our crew was on the ground from day one. We interviewed top fire officials and leading scientists. And, we learned exactly what went wrong in LA - and the ONE THING that could stop these UNSTOPPABLE fires.

#### Waking Up to Wildfires

##### Waking Up to Wildfires (Emmy-Nominated documentary, KVIE, PBS)

**Paige Bierma**, *02-21-2021*

###### Documentary Film (26:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/-xqiTB0ANlU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

###### Description

In Waking Up to Wildfires, Emmy-winning filmmaker Paige Bierma uses her camera to tell the stories of people most affected by the 2017 North Bay wildfires. We hear from survivors, firefighters, public health officials, community groups and scientists trying to make sense of it all while people struggle to recover and new fires erupt.

The UC Davis Environmental Health Sciences Center produced Waking Up to Wildfires with a grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to help shed light on the plight communities face after these types of disasters.

You're watching a condensed version (26 minutes long) that's currently airing on PBS stations across the country. To find out more or get a copy, visit our website at environmentalhealth.ucdavis.edu.
